abstract: Marine plankton diversity influences key ecosystem properties, including primary production and carbon export, and is monitored using diverse observation systems. Yet, it remains unclear whether global diversity patterns from different observation streams converge, and whether potential commonalities can guide monitoring, modelling, and conservation. Using a habitat modelling (CEPHALOPOD), we compare plankton diversity patterns across observation types and metrics, relating global open-ocean surface diversity from 330,000 observations of occurrence, abundance, biomass, and relative metagenomic reads to environmental climatologies. We find that diversity patterns converge on a latitudinal diversity gradient, with tropical oligotrophic gyres, western boundary currents and the Info-Pacific archipelago emerging as diversity hotspots. Occurrence-based estimates indicate higher diversity in eastern boundary upwellings than estimates accounting for community dominance, showing how multiple observation types provide complementary views of diversity. Surface ocean temperature, primary production, and physical transport emerge as remotely observable diversity proxies that can guide in situ sampling. Finally, diversity-ecosystem functioning relationships depend on the observation system: occurrence-based estimates highlight how diverse species can support production through complementary ecological roles, whereas abundance-, biomass-, and metagenomic-based estimates better reflect how dominant species contribute to processes such as carbon export. These findings can guide monitoring, modelling, and conservation under climate change.
